title: The Map Swelled
concept: A study in Nature Climate Change (November 20th, Zhao et al., co-author Tobias Bolch of TU Graz) used deep learning to map glacier lakes worldwide from Landsat images of about 2000 and about 2020, and people checked them by hand. Lakes touching glaciers rose by 3,567, about 35 percent, but their area only about 9 percent. The release calls Alaska's growth particularly pronounced but prints no Alaska number, so we counted the authors' open map: our count matches their world lake count exactly, Alaska's went 931 to 1,078 while their area grew about 35 percent to about 1,190 sq km, about half the world's added area from about 1 in 13 of its lakes, Vitus Lake at Bering Glacier the biggest gain (about 105 to 158 sq km). The case for yes: lake-ending glaciers lost about 66 cm of water a year against about 40 on land, and Bolch says lake contact further accelerates loss. Then the team's machine learning models weighed the factors: lake about 11, climate about 43, glacier shape about 46, for lake-ending glaciers worldwide. A real push, the smallest of the three. The release and abstract give no split for Alaska. Drawn as NIB, a drafting-pen nib that traces lakes on glowing Landsat tiles while the study's persimmon pencil checks the lines and our pine-cuffed hand counts, a world of popcorn lake chips against Alaska's lakes rising like dough, two inventory rings at Vitus Lake with our pin, two glacier fronts with water columns, a rail of three spring scales, and the release card's blank WHY row hanging as an empty fourth pan.

divergence_note: Against the last four films: 11-27 an outdoor green-slate storm with lemon lightning (hue about 52) and a teardrop glass hero on a sedge ridge; 11-26 celadon CT tile and orchid under a bone lightbox, indoors before dawn; 11-25 bone noon snow at a rail fork with railway amber; 11-24 flat July overcast on olive tundra with vermilion pins. This film is a warm umber drafting den lit from BELOW by amber-cream vellum and a lamp, with three inks each reserved to one role (ultramarine about 232 for the machine's lines, persimmon about 20 as thin pencil strokes for the study's checker, pine about 143 for OUR COUNT stamps and slips) and turquoise lake fills (about 175); persimmon sits about 12 degrees from 11-24's vermilion pins, kept to hairline pencil strokes, never fills. The hero is a steel drafting-pen nib standing on its tines, a chisel silhouette unlike 11-27's teardrop flask, 11-26's round pulse or 11-23's cylinder. Honest overlaps: 11-26 also had a backlit table (a clinical bone CT lightbox; here warm cream vellum over grey satellite tiles in a dark room), 11-24 also used overhead map shots (here the overhead view is of a drafting table, not terrain), 11-26 also lit an interior from a glowing surface (a bone CT lightbox; here a warm vellum table plus a lamp key), and the scales are nickel, not 11-27's brass; the glacier fronts are hand-drawn in this palette.

treatment.title: The Map Swelled
treatment.summary: A drafting-pen nib called NIB, the study's deep-learning tracer, draws glacier lakes on glowing Landsat tiles while the study's checker ticks its lines in persimmon pencil; our newsroom hand in a pine-green cuff counts the authors' open map and finds Alaska's lakes swelled more than they multiplied; THE CASE FOR YES is drawn at two real glacier fronts at first light; then a nickel rail of three spring scales (the team's machine learning models) weighs lake about 11, climate about 43, shape about 46, and the release card's empty WHY? tab hangs from the card's own clip as an empty pan.
treatment.judge_reasoning: Judge reasoning: the showrunner judged the four pitches directly. All four independently cast the same hero, NIB, a drafting-pen nib whose breather hole is its eye, because the tool really does draw shorelines on satellite tiles; that convergence is the strongest evidence the casting is the story's own and not a default. The Dramatist wins on structure: THE CASE FOR YES gets the whole stage (66 vs 40 cm, Bolch's quote, Alaska's swelling, Vitus's two rings) BEFORE any counterweight arrives, then a rail of three nickel spring scales for the team's machine learning models lands the answer, and the release card's blank WHY row lifts off and becomes an empty fourth pan, ALASKA'S SPLIT · NOT IN THE RELEASE OR ABSTRACT. That is the one picture that holds "a real push, the smaller one" and "Alaska's split is open" at the same time. Its loops are the cleanest: Nib's line stopping at a tile edge at 0:09 and again at the CIRCA 2020 edge in the button; the WHY row planted about 40 s and paid about 100 s.

angle.thesis: Deep learning drew the world's glacier lakes and people checked them, and because the authors posted that map we could pull the Alaska numbers the release and abstract don't print: by our count, from about 2000 to 2020 Alaska's ice-contact lakes swelled more than they multiplied (about 16 percent more lakes, about 35 percent more area, roughly half the world's added lake area), while the study's own machine learning models rank the lake as the smallest of three predictors of loss for lake-ending glaciers worldwide, a real push but not the main one, and the release and abstract give no split for Alaska.
angle.falsifiability: False if our count failed to reproduce the paper's world total (it matches exactly, c9); if Alaska's lake count grew as fast as its area (c10 +16 percent vs c11 +35 percent); if Alaska's added area were a small share of the world's (c12 about half); or if lakes rivalled climate and glacier shape as a cause (c17 about 11 percent, ranges not overlapping 43 and 46).
supporting_facts: The mechanism: deep learning drew glacier lakes worldwide from Landsat images for 2000 and 2020 (c3, c4), people checked them by hand (c5), and the whole inventory is public (c8).

The world multiplied, Alaska swelled: worldwide ice-contact lakes rose 35 percent in number (c6) but about 9 percent in area (c19); our count matches the world's lake count exactly (c9, count only) and finds Alaska's 931 to 1,078, +16 percent (c10), while their area grew about 35 percent (c11), about half the world's added area (c12) from about 1 in 13 of its ice-contact lakes (c20), Vitus Lake at Bering Glacier the biggest gain (c13).

The weight of the lake, both ways: lake-ending glaciers lose about 66 cm of water a year against about 40 on land (c14) and Bolch says contact further accelerates the loss (c15), but machine learning models give the lake about 11 percent, climate about 43, glacier shape about 46 (c16, c17).
angle.counterpoint_to_honor: Gets its own scene at full strength: lake-ending glaciers lose ice about two thirds faster (c14) and the co-author says lake contact further accelerates loss (c15), and Alaska is where lake area grew most, while the release and abstract give no split for Alaska, so the local push could be bigger than the global 11 percent. The film says plainly it's an open question and holds both: a real push, the smaller one. Our count is ours, not peer reviewed, labelled on every surface; area carries about.
angle.valence: curious, leaning celebratory about the method: a global, human-checked, open census that a small Alaska newsroom could reproduce to the lake. No hazard claim, the abstract and release make none.

runner_up_angles.angle: Analyst B, the lake is mostly a witness: Alaska's swelling lakes are a gauge of loss driven by climate and shape
runner_up_angles.why_lost: folded in as the second movement; on its own it under-sells the real accelerant (c14, c15) and loses the AI-and-open-data story the viewer can feel

runner_up_angles.angle: Analyst C, open data lets Alaska pull its own numbers from a global paper
runner_up_angles.why_lost: became the spine; on its own it risked ending on a methods brag without the cause question

runner_up_angles.angle: Analyst A, AI-first human-checked map shows swelling not multiplying, a free repeatable way to track glaciers, not an alarm
runner_up_angles.why_lost: 'free, repeatable' implies a future update the record doesn't promise (c18 the map stops at 2020); kept as the button's question

angle.cross_challenge: Round one: three analysts (mechanism, counterweight, Alaska upside). Round two: an editor red-teamed the synthesis and it was revised: dropped 'for the first time' and 'every lake', limited 'matches exactly' to the count, past tense with dates, cut 'gauge' as the study's verdict (our reading at most), put the model framing on the 11/43/46 split (c16 beside c17), one up-front OUR COUNT label, credit to the open data not to us, and promoted the world-multiplied-Alaska-swelled contrast (c19, c20) to the middle movement.

open_loop.what: Does a lake eat its glacier? Planted as a real turquoise lake lapping a white ice front at first light under the plate DOES A LAKE EAT ITS GLACIER? · BY HOW MUCH?; paid when the LAKE weight lands in its pan and its spring stretches a real but short way, LAKE ~11% · LAKE-ENDING GLACIERS · WORLDWIDE, before CLIMATE and GLACIER SHAPE stretch theirs far past it.

open_loop_2.what: What goes on the empty WHY? tab? Planted as two empty pine tabs, HOW MANY? and WHY?, snapping onto the release card's edge under PARTICULARLY PRONOUNCED IN ALASKA; our slip 931 TO 1,078 is clipped beside HOW MANY?, and WHY? is paid when it flutters into the empty pan now hanging from the survey stake at the lake-ending front, ALASKA'S SPLIT · NOT IN THE RELEASE OR ABSTRACT.
